title: Dependence of charge separation efficiency on the exciton-charge transfer offset and Gaussian disorder in organic solar cells
authors: Maik Schwuchow, Carsten Deibel, Angela Thränhardt
abstract: State-of-the-art organic solar cells increasingly rely on low-offset semiconductor blends, challenging the traditional requirement of a large energetic driving force for efficient charge separation. In these systems, the energetic offset $ΔE_{\mathrm{LE-CT}}$ between local exciton (LE) and charge-transfer (CT) states approaches the thermal energy, making exciton-CT hybridization and thermal repopulation of the exciton level critical to device performance. In this work, we directly compare a macroscopic two-state rate model with three-dimensional kinetic Monte-Carlo (kMC) simulations to investigate microscopic charge separation dynamics and the role of Gaussian energetic disorder. We demonstrate that in the absence of disorder, the analytical rate model accurately reproduces kMC predictions for the whole range of $ΔE_{\mathrm{LE-CT}}$. Specifically, the macroscopic model successfully explains horizontal shifts in the internal quantum efficiency curves that arise depending on how the energetic offset is physically realized in the constituent molecules. We show that these variations can be captured entirely through the ratio of degeneracies of the LE and CT states, respectively. Introducing Gaussian energetic disorder into the kMC simulation reveals a distinct crossover behavior depending on $ΔE_{\mathrm{LE-CT}}$. While disorder is mostly detrimental at large offsets, it can significantly boost efficiency at intermediate and low offsets. Thermalization of charge carriers within the disorder-broadened density of states creates an effective driving force allowing charge separation even at zero or negative energetic offsets.
summary: This research analyzes charge separation efficiency in organic solar cells by comparing analytical rate models with detailed kMC simulations. It demonstrates that while large offsets are traditionally favored, introducing Gaussian energetic disorder can unexpectedly boost efficiency at low offsets. This enhancement occurs because thermalization within the disordered energy landscape generates an effective driving force for charge separation.
main_problem: The study investigates how charge separation efficiency in organic solar cells depends on the energetic offset between local exciton (LE) and charge-transfer (CT) states, particularly when significant Gaussian energetic disorder is present.
main_result: Energetic disorder can significantly boost charge separation efficiency at intermediate and low offsets by creating an effective driving force through thermalization within the disordered density of states. The rate model successfully captures shifts in efficiency explained by state degeneracies.
method: The work compares results from a macroscopic two-state rate model against detailed, microscopic three-dimensional kinetic Monte-Carlo (kMC) simulations.
model_or_system: The system is an organic solar cell modeled on a 3D simple cubic lattice simulating donor-acceptor interfaces. The dynamics involve exciton hopping, charge hopping, and dissociation governed by the $\Delta E_{LE-CT}$ offset.
key_observables: Internal Quantum Efficiency (IQE), relative steady-state populations of LE and CT states, and average energy levels ($\langle 	ext{ECT} angle$).
important_parameters: Exciton-Charge Transfer Offset ($\Delta E_{LE-CT}$), Gaussian disorder strength ($\sigma_{	ext{dis}}$), and temperature ($k_B T$).
main_assumptions: The rate model assumes constant rates and ignores triplet excitons; the kMC simulations assume a linear potential gradient (1 V built-in voltage) and focus on short-circuit conditions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate IQE dependence on $\Delta E_{LE-CT}$ for different disorder strengths, showing crossover behavior. Other figures map out how average CT energy shifts with disorder strength.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the rate model's agreement with kMC in the absence of disorder. It then introduces Gaussian disorder via kMC simulations to analyze the resulting crossover behavior and the mechanism by which thermalization creates an effective driving force for charge separation.
why_interesting: This work models complex, non-equilibrium charge dynamics in a disordered solid-state material using advanced simulation techniques (kMC), directly addressing how local energetic disorder modifies fundamental electronic processes like exciton dissociation—a key topic in open quantum systems and condensed matter theory.
